title: Triples That Can Form a Triangle
statement:
You get an array sticks of non-negative stick lengths. Count the triples of positions i < j < k whose three sticks can form a triangle with positive area.

Three lengths form such a triangle exactly when the two shorter ones add up to strictly more than the longest. Triples are counted by position, so equal lengths at different positions make different triples.

examples.why: 2 + 2 equals 4, so the triangle collapses to a line. The inequality must be strict.
Every choice of three positions works, and there are 4 such choices even though the lengths are all the same.

hints: If you know which of the three is longest, two of the three triangle checks are automatically true. Sorting tells you which is longest.
After sorting, fix the longest stick c. Now you need pairs a < b to its left with a + b > c.

Two pointers on the part left of c: lo at the start, hi just before c. If sticks[lo] + sticks[hi] > c, then every lo' from lo to hi − 1 also works with hi, so add hi − lo and move hi left. Otherwise move lo right.

explain.intuition:
A triangle needs three inequalities, but once the sticks are sorted only one can fail: the two shorter sticks against the longest. So sort, then fix the longest stick at position k, and count pairs i < j < k with s[i] + s[j] > s[k].

That pair count is a classic two-pointer sweep. Start with lo = 0 and hi = k − 1. If s[lo] + s[hi] is big enough, then pairing hi with any stick from lo to hi − 1 is also big enough, because those sticks are at least s[lo]. Count all hi − lo of them at once and move hi down. If the sum is too small, the shortest stick is useless with this hi, so move lo up. Each k costs O(n), giving O(n²) overall instead of O(n³).
steps: For each k from n − 1 down to 2, set lo = 0, hi = k − 1.
While lo < hi: if s[lo] + s[hi] > s[k], add hi − lo to the count and decrease hi; otherwise increase lo.
pitfalls: Using ≥ instead of >. A flat triple like (2, 2, 4) has no area.
Fixing the smallest stick instead of the largest. Then both pointers can move the sum the same way and the counting shortcut breaks.
Removing duplicate lengths before counting. Triples are counted by position, as the third example shows.

solutions.title: Check every triple
solutions.idea: Three nested loops, testing all three triangle inequalities.

solutions.title: Sort and binary search the third side
solutions.idea: After sorting, fix the two shorter sticks i < j. Every k > j with s[k] < s[i] + s[j] works; binary search for the first one that does not.

solutions.title: Sort, fix the longest, two pointers
solutions.idea: For each longest stick, sweep two pointers over the shorter ones. A valid (lo, hi) pair means every lo' in [lo, hi) is valid too.

followups: Return the largest perimeter of any valid triangle instead of the count. Can you do better than O(n²)?
Lengths are at most 1000. How could counting how many sticks have each length help when n is huge?
